title: SEBI, NSE Sound Alarm on 'Boss Scam' and Fake Trading App Frauds
excerpt: India's markets regulator has issued a fresh warning about cybercriminals impersonating CEOs to trick employees into transferring funds, while the NSE flags AI-generated deepfake videos of its chief recommending stocks.
body:
• SEBI has warned regulated entities about the 'boss scam,' where fraudsters impersonate CEOs via WhatsApp, email, and Teams to trick employees into transferring funds.
  • The NSE flagged AI-generated deepfake videos of its MD & CEO Ashishkumar Chauhan falsely recommending stocks to investors.
  • SEBI has partnered with Google to introduce verified badges for 600+ trading apps on the Play Store and flagged over 1.33 lakh misleading social media posts this fiscal year.
  • Investors are advised to verify all investment platforms through SEBI's official portal and never act on unsolicited financial advice from social media.

SEBI Raises Red Flag on 'Boss Scam'

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) on 17 July issued a pointed warning about a cyber fraud it calls the "boss scam" — a scheme in which criminals impersonate CEOs and other senior executives to dupe employees into wiring money to fraudulent accounts.

The alert came after SEBI received intelligence from the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) about a spike in such incidents targeting finance officers and other staff at regulated entities. Fraudsters have been reaching victims through email, WhatsApp, Microsoft Teams, and social media platforms, posing as top management and issuing urgent payment instructions.

"The fraudster gets access to the finance officer's WhatsApp account and then contacts accounts or finance employees, instructing them to make immediate payments to specified mule bank accounts."

— SEBI advisory, 17 July 2026

"More than 600 apps now carry the badge — a practical tool for investors to distinguish legitimate platforms from clones designed to siphon money."

A particularly insidious variant of the scam involves sending malware files disguised as routine documents. Once opened, the malware hijacks WhatsApp Web sessions, giving attackers direct access to the victim's messaging account — and from there, a credible channel to order payments.

SEBI has directed all regulated entities to ensure that no funds are transferred solely on the basis of instructions received through social media platforms, and to implement multi-step verification procedures for all payment requests.

NSE Flags Deepfake Videos of Its CEO

In a related development, the National Stock Exchange (NSE) has cautioned investors against AI-generated deepfake audio and video clips featuring its Managing Director and CEO, Ashishkumar Chauhan. The fabricated clips use sophisticated technology to imitate Chauhan's voice and facial expressions, falsely showing him recommending specific stocks.

The exchange has been working to get the videos taken down from social media platforms. NSE stressed that none of its employees are authorised to recommend stocks, and that all official communications come only through its verified website and social media handles.

A Growing Arsenal of Digital Fraud

These warnings are the latest in an intensifying campaign by Indian regulators against new-age investment fraud. In March 2026, SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey disclosed that the regulator had flagged over 1.33 lakh misleading social media posts related to the securities market in the current fiscal year alone, and identified 66 fake trading apps that were subsequently removed from app stores.

SEBI also partnered with Google to roll out "verified" badges on the Google Play Store for trading apps operated by registered entities. More than 600 apps now carry the badge — a practical tool for investors to distinguish legitimate platforms from clones designed to siphon money. The regulator's in-house AI surveillance tool, Sudarshan, launched in 2025, now tracks misleading content across multiple Indian languages in real time.

An MoU with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) is also in the works to create a unified anti-fraud response across digital platforms.

What This Means for the Indian Diaspora

For Indian investors abroad, the warnings carry particular weight. Diaspora investors frequently manage portfolios remotely through digital platforms and are prime targets for fake trading apps and phishing schemes that exploit distance and time-zone gaps. Fraudsters running WhatsApp-based "investment advisory" groups have repeatedly targeted NRIs with promises of guaranteed returns on Indian equities, only to vanish after collecting funds.

SEBI's verified badge initiative and the growing crackdown on finfluencers offer some guardrails, but the onus remains on individual investors to verify every platform and advisory before committing capital. The regulator's investor complaint portal (scores.sebi.gov.in) and the national cyber helpline (1930) are available for reporting suspected fraud.

What Comes Next

With India now home to over 140 million unique investors — most of them digital-first — the scale of the fraud surface is enormous. SEBI's multi-pronged approach, combining regulatory alerts, platform partnerships, AI surveillance, and cross-ministry coordination, signals that the regulator views digital fraud not as a fringe issue but as a systemic risk. How quickly these measures translate into reduced fraud volumes will be the real test.
